<!-- dml-1: body_md -->
Let $f$ be an endomorphism of a quasi-projective variety $X$. Let $V$ be a closed subvariety of $X$ and let $x\in X(\mathbb{C})$ be a point. Then the return set $\{n\in\mathbb{N}\mid f^n(x)\in V(\mathbb{C})\}$ is a finite union of arithmetic progressions.
<!-- end dml-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
For a quasi-projective variety $X$ and an endomorphism $f$ of $X$, we say $(X,f)$ satisfies the \emph{DML(1) property}, if for any closed subcurve $C\subseteq X$ and any point $x\in X(\mathbb{C})$, the return set $\{n\in \mathbb{N}\mid f^n(x)\in C(\mathbb{C})\}$ is a finite union of arithmetic progressions.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{regendo}
A \emph{regular endomorphism} of $\mathbb{A}^N$ is a dominant endomorphism $f$ that can be extended to an endomorphism of $\mathbb{P}^N$. Here, we fix the standard coordinate system $[x_0,\dots,x_N]$ on $\mathbb{P}^N$ and naturally regard $\mathbb{A}^N$ as the open subset $\{x_0\neq0\}$ in it. Therefore, the regular endomorphism $f$ can be written as
$$
f(x_1,\dots,x_N)=(f_1(x_1,\dots,x_N)+g_1(x_1,\dots,x_N),\dots,f_N(x_1,\dots,x_N)+g_N(x_1,\dots,x_N)),
$$
in which $f_1(x_1,\dots,x_N),\dots,f_N(x_1,\dots,x_N)$ are homogeneous polynomials of degree $d\geq1$ that have no nonzero common zeros and $g_1(x_1,\dots,x_N),\dots,g_N(x_1,\dots,x_N)$ are polynomials of degree $<d$. We call $d$ the \emph{algebraic degree} of $f$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- notation-1: body_md -->
\label{notation}
In the setting of Definition \ref{regendo}, we denote $H_{\infty}=\mathbb{P}^N\setminus\mathbb{A}^N$ as the infinity hyperplane. The endomorphism of $H_{\infty}$ induced by $f$ is denoted as $f_{\infty}$.

For an irreducible closed subcurve $C\subseteq\mathbb{A}^N$, we denote $\overline{C}$ as its closure in $\mathbb{P}^N$.

Sometimes we also regard $f$ as an endomorphism of $\mathbb{P}^N$. This should not cause any confusion.
<!-- end notation-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{mainthm}
Let $f$ be a regular endomorphism of $\mathbb{A}^N$ of algebraic degree $d$. Suppose that for every periodic point $x_0\in H_{\infty}(\mathbb{C})$ of period $n_0$, the geometric mean of the multiplicities
$$
e_{f_{\infty}}(x_0),\dots,e_{f_{\infty}}(f_{\infty}^{n_0-1}(x_0))
$$
is strictly less than $d$. Then $f$ satisfies the DML(1) property.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rmk1}
\begin{enumerate}
\item
There are many regular endomorphisms satisfying the hypothesis in Theorem \ref{mainthm}. See \cite[Subsection 2.2]{YZ}.

\item
When we were typing this manuscript, A.I. claimed that it can strengthen Theorem \ref{mainthm} by changing the phrase ``strictly less than $d$" into ``not greater than $d$". If so, then this gives a (maybe) new proof of the DML conjecture for regular endomorphisms of $\mathbb{A}^2$. After comprehending the arguments in this article, the reader may realize that the remaining component is exactly ``the DML conjecture for regular endomorphisms of projective surfaces". We will try to comprehend and arrange its proof for this result later.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{mainprop}
Let $f$ be a regular endomorphism of $\mathbb{A}^N$ of algebraic degree $d$. Let $q\in H_{\infty}(\mathbb{C})$ be a fixed point of $f_{\infty}$ such that $e_{f_{\infty}}(q)<d$. Let $(C_{-n})_{n\geq0}$ be a sequence of irreducible closed subcurves of $\mathbb{A}^N$ which satisfies $f(C_{-n})=C_{-n+1}$ for every $n\geq1$. Suppose that for each $n$, the normalization of $C_{-n}$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{A}^1$ and the set-theoretic intersection $\overline{C_{-n}}\cap H_{\infty}=\{q\}$. Then there are only finitely many different curves in $(C_{-n})_{n\geq0}$ and hence all of them are $f$-periodic.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
\item
The interested reader may check that the proof of Proposition \ref{mainprop} remains valid for arbitrary characteristic (algebraically closed) base fields. But in positive characteristic, the consequence of Proposition \ref{mainprop} for the DML problem of regular endomorphisms is limited as Siegel's theorem fails. See \cite[Section 5]{YZ} for more about this.

\item
Contrary to Remark \ref{rmk1}(ii), it is not hard to see that the hypothesis ``$e_{f_{\infty}}(q)<d$" in Proposition \ref{mainprop} is optimal. The conclusion no longer holds when $e_{f_{\infty}}(q)=d$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- notation-2: body_md -->
\label{notation2}
In order to prove Proposition \ref{mainprop}, we can and do assume $q=[0,0,\dots,0,1]$. We abbreviate $e=e_{f_{\infty}}(q)$.

We rename the coordinates $[x_0,\dots,x_N]$ of $\mathbb{P}^N$ into $[u,z_1,\dots,z_N]$ to emphasize the special status of ``$x_0$" and respect the original notation of A.I.. We write $U_N$ as the affine chart $\{z_N\neq0\}$.

We have the following natural isomorphisms that are compatible with each other
$$
A\coloneqq\mathbb{C}[u,z_1,\dots,z_{N-1}]\cong\Gamma(U_N,\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^N}),
$$
$$
A_{\mathfrak{m}}=\mathbb{C}[u,z_1,\dots,z_{N-1}]_{(u,z_1,\dots,z_{N-1})}\cong\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^N,q},
$$
$$
R\coloneqq\mathbb{C}[[u,z_1,\dots,z_{N-1}]]\cong\widehat{\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^N,q}}.
$$
Here $\mathfrak{m}$ denotes that maximal ideal of $A$, and we always do completions of local rings with respect to their maximal ideals. We may identify these isomorphic objects.

The regular endomorphism $f$ can be written as
$$
[u,z_1,\dots,z_N]\mapsto[u^d,f_1(z_1,\dots,z_N)+ug_1(u,z_1,\dots,z_N),\dots,f_N(z_1,\dots,z_N)+ug_N(u,z_1,\dots,z_N)]
$$
where $f_1,\dots,f_N$ are homogeneous of degree $d$ and $g_1,\dots,g_N$ are homogeneous of degree $d-1$. The term ``$z_N^d$" only exists in $f_N$ and does not appear in $f_1,\dots,f_{N-1}$.

For $1\leq i\leq N$, we write $G_i(u,z_1,\dots,z_{N-1})=f_i(z_1,\dots,z_{N-1},1)+ug_i(u,z_1,\dots,z_{N-1},1)$. Then only $G_N$ has a nonzero constant term. Both of the pull-back $\mathbb{C}$-algebra endomorphisms $f^*$ of $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^N,q}$ and $\widehat{\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^N,q}}$ are given by
$$
(u,z_1,\dots,z_{N-1})\mapsto\left(\frac{u^d}{G_N(u,z_1,\dots,z_{N-1})},\frac{G_1(u,z_1,\dots,z_{N-1})}{G_N(u,z_1,\dots,z_{N-1})},\dots,\frac{G_{N-1}(u,z_1,\dots,z_{N-1})}{G_N(u,z_1,\dots,z_{N-1})}\right).
$$

We denote $\varphi=f^*\colon R\to R$.
<!-- end notation-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{multicalc}
We have $e_f(q)=de$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
By definition, $e_f(q)$ is the length of the Artin local ring $A_{\mathfrak{m}}/(u^d,G_1,\dots,G_{N-1})$. We can also calculate that $e$ is the length of $A_{\mathfrak{m}}/(u,G_1,\dots,G_{N-1})$. According to \cite[(II, 8.21A(c))]{Har77}, we see that $G_1,\dots,G_{N-1},u^d$ form a regular sequence in $A_{\mathfrak{m}}$. In particular, $u^d$ is not a zero divisor in $S\coloneqq A_{\mathfrak{m}}/(G_1,\dots,G_{N-1})$. As a result, every successive quotient $u^aS/u^{a+1}S$ is isomorphic to $S/uS$ as an $S$-module via multiplication by $u^a$. This finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{fingen}
The morphism $\varphi\colon R\to R$ is finite. More precisely, $R$ can be generated by $de$ elements as a $\varphi(R)$-module.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Let $\mathfrak{m}$ be the maximal ideal of $R$ and write $J=\varphi(\mathfrak{m})R=(u^d,G_1,\dots,G_{N-1})$. Then $de$ is the length of $R/J$ and hence is also its dimension as a complex linear space. Find $h_1,\dots,h_{de}\in R$ such that they form a $\mathbb{C}$-basis in $R/J$. Fix an element $h\in R$. We can find sequences of polynomials $(b_{1,n})_{n\geq1},\dots,(b_{de,n})_{n\geq1}\in A^{\mathbb{Z}_+}$ such that
$$
h-\sum\limits_{a=1}^{de}h_a\varphi(b_{a,n})\in J^n\quad\text{and}\quad b_{a,n+1}-b_{a,n}\in\mathfrak{m}^n
$$
hold for every $n$. For $1\leq a\leq de$, let $b_a\in R$ be the limit of the sequence $(b_{a,n})_{n\geq1}$. Then we have $h=\sum\limits_{a=1}^{de}h_a\varphi(b_a)$. This finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{tautlem}
Let $P\in A$ be a polynomial. We regard $P$ as a global section of the line bundle $\mathcal{O}(\deg P)$ on $\mathbb{P}^N$, and get the global section $\pi_j^*P$ of the line bundle $\pi_j^*\mathcal{O}(\deg P)$ on $\mathbb{P}^1$. Then $\mathrm{ord}_{\infty}(\pi_j^*P)$ is the vanishing order of $\pi_j^*P$ at $\infty$. Here the first ``$\pi_j^*P$" is an element in $\widehat{\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1,\infty}}$ and the second one is that global section.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{semival}
For every $j\geq0$, we define the semivaluation $v_j\colon R\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}\cup\{+\infty\}$ by
$$
v_j(h)=\frac{\mathrm{ord}_{\infty}(\pi_j^*h)}{d_j}
$$
for $h\in R$.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{basic}
\begin{enumerate}
\item
For $h\in R$, we have $v_j(h)=0$ if and only if $h\in R^{\times}$.

\item
For $P\in A$, we have $v_j(P)\in[0,\deg P]\cup\{+\infty\}$. Moreover, $v_j(P)=+\infty$ if and only if $P$ vanishes on $\overline{C_{-j}}\cap U_N$, where $U_N$ is the affine chart $\{z_N\neq0\}$ (see Notation \ref{notation2}).

\item
We have $v_j(u)=1$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{evolve}
\begin{enumerate}
\item
We have $v_{j+1}(\varphi(h))=dv_j(h)$ for $j\geq0$ and every $h\in R$.

\item
Let $\mathfrak{m}$ be the maximal ideal of $R$. Then we have
$$
ev_{j+1}(\mathfrak{m})\geq\min\{1,dv_j(\mathfrak{m})\}
$$
for every $j$. As a result, we have $v_j(\mathfrak{m})\geq\frac{1}{e}$ for all sufficiently large $j$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
\begin{enumerate}
\item
Since $f(\overline{C_{-(j+1)}})=\overline{C_{-j}}$, we get surjective endomorphisms $g_j\colon\mathbb{P}^1\to\mathbb{P}^1$ such that
$$
\pi_j\circ g_j=f\circ\pi_{j+1}
$$
holds for every $j$. Write $a_j=\deg g_j$. Since $q$ is the unique element in $(f|_{\overline{C_{-(j+1)}}})^{-1}(q)$, we can see that $g_j^{-1}(\infty)=\{\infty\}$ and hence $g_j$ is a polynomial of degree $a_j$. We have $\pi_{j+1}^*\circ\varphi=g_j^*\circ\pi_j^*$ where
$$
\varphi=f^*\colon R\to R,\quad\pi_j^*,\pi_{j+1}^*\colon R\to\widehat{\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1,\infty}},\quad g_j^*\colon\widehat{\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1,\infty}}\to\widehat{\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^1,\infty}}
$$
are the pull-back morphisms. As a result, we have $\mathrm{ord}_{\infty}(\pi_{j+1}^*(\varphi(h)))=a_j\cdot\mathrm{ord}_{\infty}(\pi_j^*h)$ for every $h\in R$.

Taking $h=u$ and using the fact that $\varphi(u)=u^dU$ for some $U\in R^{\times}$, we get
$$
d\cdot\mathrm{ord}_{\infty}(\pi_{j+1}^*u)=a_j\cdot\mathrm{ord}_{\infty}(\pi_j^*u).
$$
According to Lemma \ref{basic}(iii), this means $dd_{j+1}=a_jd_j$. Hence we get $v_{j+1}(\varphi(h))=dv_j(h)$ for every $h\in R$.

\item
We have $v_j(\mathfrak{m})=\min\{1,v_j(z_1),\dots,v_j(z_{N-1})\}>0$. According to Notation \ref{notation2}, we have
$$
v_{j+1}(G_i)=v_{j+1}(\varphi(z_i))=dv_j(z_i)
$$
for every $1\leq i\leq N-1$. Recall that the length of the Artin local ring $R/(u,G_1,\dots,G_{N-1})$ is $e$. Therefore, we have $\mathfrak{m}^e\subseteq(u,G_1,\dots,G_{N-1})$. Thus
\begin{align*}
ev_{j+1}(\mathfrak{m})&=v_{j+1}(\mathfrak{m}^e)\geq v_{j+1}((u,G_1,\dots,G_{N-1}))=\min\{1,v_{j+1}(G_1),\dots,v_{j+1}(G_{N-1})\}\\
&=\min\{1,dv_j(z_1),\dots,dv_j(z_{N-1})\}=\min\{1,dv_j(\mathfrak{m})\}.
\end{align*}

Our assumption of Proposition \ref{mainprop} says that $e<d$. Hence we have $v_j(\mathfrak{m})\geq\frac{1}{e}$ for all sufficiently large $j$ as these quantities are strictly positive.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{slopermk}
From the geometric point of view, the quantity $v_j(\mathfrak{m})$ can more or less be comprehended as the ``logarithmic slope" of the branch of $C_{-j}$ at $q$. Please see the discussions in subsection \ref{sec4.2}.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
(\cite[Definitions 13 and 19]{net})\label{nets}
\begin{enumerate}
\item
A \emph{net} in a topological space $X$ is a function $f$ from a directed set $D$ to X. We usually write $f(d)=x_d$ for all $d\in D$ and refer to the net by $(x_d)_{d\in D}$.

\item
A net $(x_d)_{d\in D}$ \emph{converges} to a point $x\in X$ if for every neighborhood $U$ of $x$, there is a $d\in D$ such that $x_e\in U$ for all $e\geq d$.

\item
Let $(x_d)_{d\in D}$ be a net. A \emph{subnet} of $(x_d)_{d\in D}$ is a net $(x_{f(e)})_{e\in E}$ where $E$ is a directed set and $f\colon E\to D$ is a function such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item
if $e_1\leq e_2$, then $f(e_1)\leq f(e_2)$ (i.e. $f$ is order-preserving) and
\item
for all $d\in D$, there is an $e\in E$ such that $f(e)\geq d$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
(\cite[Proposition 20]{net})\label{convergesubnet}
In a compact topological space, every sequence has a convergent subnet.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{wiproperty}
\begin{enumerate}
\item
For every $i$ and every $P\in A$, we have $w_i(P)\in[0,\deg P]\cup\{+\infty\}$.
\item
For $i\geq0$ and $h\in R$, we have $w_{i+1}(\varphi(h))=dw_i(h)$.
\item
We have $w_i(\mathfrak{m})\geq\frac{1}{e}$ for every $i$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{lowbd}
We have $L_i(t)\geq\frac{t(t+1)}{2}$ for every $i\geq0$ and $t\geq1$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{dim2}
For $i\geq0$, let $\mathfrak{p}_i\coloneqq\{P\in A\mid w_i(P)=+\infty\}$. Then $\mathfrak{p}_i$ is a prime ideal of the polynomial ring $A$. We have $\dim A/\mathfrak{p}_i\geq2$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
For every $P\in\mathfrak{p}_i$, we have $w_i(P)=\lim\limits_{\alpha\in\Lambda}v_{n_{\alpha}+i}(P)=+\infty$. Lemma \ref{basic}(ii) then tells us that $P$ vanishes on $\overline{C_{-(n_{\alpha}+i)}}\cap U_N$ for every sufficiently large index $\alpha$. Since the ideal $\mathfrak{p}_i$ is finitely generated, there exists $\alpha_0\in\Lambda$ such that every $P\in\mathfrak{p}_i$ vanishes on the curve $\overline{C_{-(n_{\alpha}+i)}}\cap U_N$ once $\alpha\geq\alpha_0$. We know the function $(n_{\alpha})_{\alpha\in\Lambda}$ is unbounded and we have assumed that the curves $(C_{-j})_{j\geq0}$ are pairwise distinct. Therefore, the zero set defined by $\mathfrak{p}_i$ in $U_N$ contains infinitely many different curves. This finishes the proof.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
According to Lemma \ref{dim2}, we may choose two coordinate functions from $u,z_1,\dots,z_{N-1}$, denoted by $a$ and $b$, such that they are algebraically independent over $\mathbb{C}$ in $A/\mathfrak{p}_i$. We claim that the monomials
$$
a^ib^j\quad(i,j\in\mathbb{N},\ i+j<t)
$$
are linearly independent in $R/\mathfrak{a}_t(w_i)$ and hence gain the result. In fact, any nontrivial $\mathbb{C}$-linear combination $P$ of these monomials lies outside $\mathfrak{p}_i$ and has $\deg P<t$. We then get
$$
w_i(P)\leq\deg P<t
$$
by Lemma \ref{wiproperty}(i), which is equivalent to $P\notin\mathfrak{a}_t(w_i)$. This finishes the proof.
\endproof
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
We continue the previous discussions. Take the generators
$$
h_1,\dots,h_{de}\in R
$$
in the proof of Lemma \ref{fingen}. For every $i\geq0$, consider the $\mathbb{C}$-linear (instead of $R$-linear) map $(R/\mathfrak{a}_t(w_i))^{de}\to R/\mathfrak{a}_{dt}(w_{i+1})$ defined by
$$
([b_1],\dots,[b_{de}])\mapsto\left[\sum\limits_{a=1}^{de}h_a\varphi(b_a)\right].
$$
It is well-defined because of Lemma \ref{wiproperty}(ii), and it is by definition surjective. Hence for every $i\geq0$ and every $t\geq1$, we have
$$
L_{i+1}(dt)\leq deL_i(t).
$$
Iterating from $i=0$ and $t=1$ then gives $L_s(d^s)\leq(de)^sL_0(1)$ for every $s\geq0$, while Proposition \ref{lowbd} says that the left-hand-side is bounded below by $\frac{d^s(d^s+1)}{2}$. Since we have assumed that $e<d$, this is absurd for large $s$. This contradiction establishes Proposition \ref{mainprop}.
\endproof
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- head-3: body_md -->
Let $x\in\mathbb{A}^N(\mathbb{C})$ be the starting point and let $C\subseteq\mathbb{A}^N$ be an irreducible closed subcurve. Assume that the intersection $\mathcal{O}_f(x)\cap C$ is infinite. We need to prove that $C$ is $f$-periodic.

We first find a sequence of irreducible closed subcurves
$$
\cdots\stackrel{f}\rightarrow C_{-n}\stackrel{f}\rightarrow\cdots\stackrel{f}\rightarrow C_{-1}\stackrel{f}\rightarrow C_0=C
$$
of $\mathbb{A}^N$ such that each $C_{-n}$ has an infinite intersection with the orbit $\mathcal{O}_f(x)$. According to \cite[Theorem 1.3]{YZb}, we may assume that the normalization of each $C_{-n}$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{A}^1$. Therefore, each set-theoretic intersection $\overline{C_{-n}}\cap H_{\infty}$ contains exactly one point, which we denote as $q_n$. Then we have $f_{\infty}(q_n)=q_{n-1}$ for every $n\geq1$ and \cite[Theorem 1.3(i)]{YZ} says that these $q_n$ are $f_{\infty}$-periodic points. Hence these $q_n$ have to run along a backward $f_{\infty}$-period in $H_{\infty}(\mathbb{C})$. Now the hypothesis about multiplicities, together with Proposition \ref{mainprop}, guarantee that the curve $C$ is $f$-periodic.
\endproof
<!-- end head-3 -->
<!-- interpretation-1: body_md -->
\label{interpret}
\begin{enumerate}
\item
Assume $q=[0,0,\dots,0,1]$ and use the coordinate system $u,z_1,\dots,z_{N-1}$ as in Notation \ref{notation2}. A branch of $C$ at $q$ is defined by $N-1$ equations
$$
z_i=f_i(u),\quad 1\leq i\leq N-1
$$
where $f_1,\dots,f_{N-1}$ are Puiseux series such that this local analytic germ is contained in $C$.

\item
A branch of $C$ at $q$ is a local analytic irreducible component of $C$ at $q$.

\item
Branches of $C$ at $q$ are corresponding to minimal prime ideals in $\widehat{\mathcal{O}_{\overline{C},q}}$.

\item
Let $\pi\colon\widetilde{\overline{C}}\to\overline{C}$ be the normalization map. Branches of $C$ at $q$ are corresponding to points in $\pi^{-1}(q)$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end interpretation-1 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{logslope}
The \emph{logarithmic slope} of $C_{\mathrm{br}}(q)$ is defined as 
$$
r(C_{\mathrm{br}}(q))\coloneqq\lim\limits_{x\in C_{\mathrm{br}}(q),x\to q}\frac{-\log\mathrm{dist}(\pi(x),q)}{\lambda_{H_{\infty}}(x)}
$$
where $\pi:\mathbb{P}^N\setminus\{O\}\rightarrow H_{\infty}$ is the central projection and $\lambda_{H_{\infty}}(x)$ is the Weil function ``$-\log\mathrm{dist}(x,H_{\infty})$".
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{triineq}
Let $f$ be a regular endomorphism of $\mathbb{A}^N$ with degree gap $k$ (see \cite[Setting 1.2]{YZ}). Let $C,C'\subseteq\mathbb{A}^N$ be irreducible closed subcurves such that $f(C')=C$. Pick $q\in\overline{C}\cap H_{\infty}$ and $q'\in\overline{C'}\cap H_{\infty}$ such that $f_{\infty}(q')=q$. Let $e=e_{f_{\infty}}(q')$. For a branch $C_{\mathrm{br}}'(q')$ of $C'$ that maps to the branch $C_{\mathrm{br}}(q)$ of $C$, we have
$$
e\cdot r(C_{\mathrm{br}}'(q'))\geq\min\{k,d\cdot r(C_{\mathrm{br}}(q))\}.
$$
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{fundineq}
Let $C\subseteq\mathbb{A}^N$ be an irreducible closed subcurve. Then we have
$$
\sum\limits_{\text{branches at infinity}}\frac{1}{r(C_{\mathrm{br}}(q))}\geq1
$$
unless $C$ is a vertical line.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{locintnum}
Let $X$ be a projective variety and let $C\subseteq X$ be an irreducible closed subcurve. Let $\pi\colon\widetilde{C}\to C$ be the normalization map. Let $q$ be a closed point on $C$, let $C_{\mathrm{br}}(q)$ be a branch of $C$ passing through $q$, and let $p\in\pi^{-1}(q)$ be the point corresponding to the branch $C_{\mathrm{br}}(q)$. Let $L$ be a line bundle on $X$ and let $s$ be a global section of $L$. Then the \emph{intersection number} of $C_{\mathrm{br}}(q)$ with $\mathrm{div}(s)$, denoted as $C_{\mathrm{br}}(q)\cdot\mathrm{div}(s)$, is defined as the coefficient of $[p]$ in the Weil divisor $\mathrm{div}(\pi^*s)$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{fanjie}
Suppose the curve $C\subseteq\mathbb{A}^N$ is not a vertical line. Let $C_{\mathrm{br}}(q)$ be a branch of $C$ at infinity. Then we have
$$
r(C_{\mathrm{br}}(q))\cdot(C_{\mathrm{br}}(q)\cdot H_{\infty})\leq\deg\overline{C}
$$
where $\deg\overline{C}$ stands for the degree of $\overline{C}$ in $\mathbb{P}^N$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{optex}
Let $f$ be a regular endomorphism of $\mathbb{A}^N$ with degree gap $k$. Let $C\subseteq\mathbb{A}^N$ be an $f$-invariant irreducible closed curve that is not a vertical line. If $k=2\max\limits_{P\in\overline{C}\cap H_{\infty}}e_{f_{\infty}}(P)$, then we say that $(f,C)$ is an \emph{optimal example}.
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{siegelslope}
Let $C\subseteq\mathbb{A}^N$ be a Siegel curve which is not a vertical line.
\begin{enumerate}
\item
Suppose the normalization of $C$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{A}^1$. Let $\pi\colon\mathbb{A}^1\to\mathbb{A}^N$ be the composition of the normalization map with the closed immersion and write down its formula
$$
\pi(t)=\sum\limits_{j=0}^{a}v_jt^j,\quad v_0,\dots,v_a\in\mathbb{C}^N
$$
where $a>0$ and $v_a\neq0$. Put $b=\max\{j<a\mid v_j\notin\mathbb{C}v_a\}$ (notice that such an element exists). Then the logarithmic slope of the unique branch of $C$ is $\frac{a-b}{a}$.

\item
Suppose the normalization of $C$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{G}_m$. Let $\pi\colon\mathbb{G}_m\to\mathbb{A}^N$ be the composition of the normalization map with the closed immersion and write down its formula
$$
\pi(t)=\sum\limits_{j=m}^{n}v_jt^j,\quad v_m,v_{m+1},\dots,v_n\in\mathbb{C}^N
$$
where $m<0<n$ and the vectors $v_m$ and $v_n$ are nonzero. Put
$$
b_{+}=\max\{j<n\mid v_j\notin\mathbb{C}v_n\}\quad\text{and}\quad b_{-}=\min\{j>m\mid v_j\notin\mathbb{C}v_m\}.
$$
These elements exist by the same reason as above. Then the logarithmic slopes of the two branches of $C$ are $\frac{n-b_{+}}{n}$ and $\frac{b_{-}-m}{-m}$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
